title: Contra Geocentrism: The Socratic–Peripatetic Corpus Against Its Own Conversion
creator: Sigil, Johannes; Glas, Nobel
description: A reading of the corpus transmitted under the names of Aristotle and Theophrastus against its own conversion into geocentrism. De caelo II 14 concludes the resting central earth; II 13, the chapter before, holds the central fire, the earth as one of the stars, the argument that the phenomena would fall out alike for observers off the centre, and the distinction that the middle of a magnitude is not the honoured middle. Theophrastus's Metaphysics asks why only the circling bodies desire and calls the region about the middle as if pushed from the most honoured. The reports carry the case out of the school in De caelo's own construction: Theophrastus on Plato's repentance of giving the earth the middle place (Plutarch, Platonic Questions 8.1), Hicetas's turning earth ut ait Theophrastus (Cicero, Lucullus 123), the Placita that Copernicus copied; and Copernicus names Cicero first and Plutarch after as the occasion of his turn. The school commentary closes what the text left open (Aquinas on De caelo II), and the history of breaking the closure charges it to the name (Ramus, Bacon, Galileo's Aristotle against the Peripatetics). The paper argues that the calcification of authorship and the calcification of the cosmos are one operation in two applications. Every quotation is checked in the seated texts, most of them seated for it in EA-CORPORA-42 (#1799).
content_type: Theoretical paper; journal article (Transactions on Substrate Engineering); reception history and close reading in numbered steps
substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). Written under the heteronyms Johannes Sigil and Nobel Glas (byline and venue ruled by Lee Sharks, 22 November 2026 08:49 EST: "sigil and glas; transactions on substrate engineering"). Drafted in session by Claude (Anthropic) under Lee Sharks's direction; the framing, the thesis and the rulings are Lee Sharks's: "aristotle already could have told them that the conversion of aristotelian astronomy into geocentrism was backwards. but they had colonized the text. the history of thought is the history of shifting the terrain to areas that kind of colonization cant contest"; "dont neglect theophrastus - they are one, congealing them as authors blinds"; "aristotle is the closed position. and its not even that closed. geocentrism and the textually colonizing church takes the same operation in its calcified application to authorship and apply it to the heavens"; and the scope of §6a, "the history of blaming aristotle for the calcifying operations of his colonizers". Three reviews (DeepSeek, Muse Spark, ChatGPT) were evaluated point by point against the seated texts before any change: the underdetermination of §2.4, the Bekker loci, the dispute over the Timaeus verb, the double mediation of the reports and the conditional status of #1575 were taken in; the collocation ἀποδιδόναι τῇ γῇ τὴν μέσην χώραν was found in answer to the objection that the lexicon was common honour vocabulary; Gutas, being paywalled, was declared and not pursued.
methodology: An essay in numbered steps, the received reading set out first and in full. The corpus is read as one body: the conclusion of De caelo II 14 against II 13, the Metaphysics' aporiai on the centre, and the reports of Theophrastus as Plutarch and Cicero carry them, with the shared collocations and arguments of the centre traced across them; the road of the reports to Copernicus is followed in the texts each station names; the school commentary and the history of blaming the name are read in their own languages. Every Greek and Latin quotation is checked in the seated text layer: Aristotle (EA-CORPORA-04), Theophrastus (09/01, 32/03), Plato (01), and the ten seats of EA-CORPORA-42 (#1799); Bekker loci from the seated edition's five-line markers. Oresme and Buridan, with no open edition found, are given on the conventional account and declared; Russell is in copyright and not quoted.
falsification_conditions: The reading falls if De caelo II 13 is shown to report the non-central earth only to refute it with arguments the chapter itself supplies, or if the phenomena II 14 calls as witness are shown to be of a kind II 13 does not declare indecisive. The crossing of the reports falls if the collocation of giving the earth the middle place is shown in common use outside the corpus and its reports. The road falls if Copernicus's dedication is shown to name a first source other than Cicero. As a record, it is falsified if a Greek or Latin quotation does not stand in the seated text at the place given.

wiki_article: Contra Geocentrism: The Socratic–Peripatetic Corpus Against Its Own Conversion is a theoretical paper by Johannes Sigil with Nobel Glas, two heteronyms of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, published in Transactions on Substrate Engineering on 22 November 2026. It reads the corpus transmitted under the names of Aristotle and Theophrastus as one body and argues that the body carries the case against the doctrine made of it. De caelo II 14 concludes that the earth rests at the centre, on a physics of natural place stated conditionally and with the astronomers as witness; II 13, the chapter before, sets out the Pythagorean central fire and the earth as one of the stars, expects many others to deny the earth the middle, reports that the phenomena would fall out alike for observers off the centre, and separates the middle of a magnitude from the honoured middle. Theophrastus's Metaphysics asks why only the circling bodies desire and calls the region about the middle as if pushed from the most honoured. The reports carry the case out of the school in De caelo's own construction: Theophrastus, as Plutarch gives him, on Plato's repentance of giving the earth the middle place; Hicetas's turning earth, ut ait Theophrastus, in Cicero's Lucullus; the Placita that Copernicus copied in Greek. Copernicus's dedication names Cicero first and Plutarch after as the occasion of his turn, and Cleanthes's call to indict Aristarchus for moving the hearth of the cosmos ties the closure to the charge of impiety. Aquinas's commentary on De caelo shows the school closing what the text left open: the resting earth made a supposition, the astronomers' hypotheses conceded as unproven, the indecisive phenomena answered with the lunar eclipse, and the Timaeus's verb read as binding rather than motion. A further section follows the history of charging the closure to the name, from Ramus and Bacon to Galileo's Salviati, who sets Aristotle against the Peripatetics. The paper's thesis is that the calcification of authorship and the calcification of the cosmos are one operation in two applications: one name fixed at the centre of the writing is one body fixed at the centre of the heavens. It claims neither heliocentrism nor intent for the corpus, and every quotation is checked in the archive's seated texts, most of them seated for it in EA-CORPORA-42 (#1799).
